articles.title_orig: Trump’s tough-on-China talk was always just an act
articles.title_zh: Trump’s tough-on-China talk was always just an act
articles.content_orig:
Don’t you wish you could administer truth serum to Laura Ingraham, Steve Bannon or the dozens of other Trumpists who proclaimed their belief in Trump’s “toughness” on the People’s Republic of China? Remember how they used to talk? In 2019, the late Lou Dobbs opened his broadcast one night on Fox Business this way:
“For far too long Communist China has been cheating the United States on trade. President Trump has made it clear: The failure of previous presidents to aggressively represent U.S. interests in foreign policy and economic policy has ended, and President Trump made believers out of the Chinese today.”
Trump’s rhetoric on “Chy-na” was feverish. They were waging “economic war” on us. They were “raping” our country. They were sending us the “China virus” or the “Kung Flu.” Trump’s supposed hawkishness on China was a selling point with working-class men. Here was a foreign scapegoat for the loss of manufacturing jobs. The focus on China justified a whole school of foreign policy advisers, led by Elbridge Colby, currently the undersecretary of defense for policy, joined by Pete Hegseth, JD Vance, Josh Hawley and Ron DeSantis, who favored limiting assistance to Ukraine in the name of keeping our powder dry for China.
What do these faux-hawks really think as they contemplate Trump’s upcoming summit with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and (if Trump can swing it) Kim Jong-un? That he’s tough? Good God.
The West prevailed over the Communist world in the Cold War for many reasons — communism makes countries poorer, for one thing-but a key factor was our superior technology. We maintained that dominance by export controls to keep American-derived knowledge out of the hands of those who wished us ill.
We are not today in a Cold War with China, but China is the most powerful repressive country on the planet, and one whose propaganda ceaselessly agitates against the U.S. The China hawks are right to be wary of China, though wrong in just about every other way.
But Trump, hyperventilating threats notwithstanding, is not a China hawk, nor is he a dove. Those categories don’t apply to him, because they imply an interest in policy and in the nation. Trump doesn’t make decisions that way. His chief focus — and, frankly, his only real concern-can be found in the shaving mirror.
The Nvidia scandal (I’m referring to the Trump administration’s actions, not the honey trap) is merely the capstone on the second-term pattern.
Like most bullies, Trump kisses up and punches down. As soon as someone punches back, Trump becomes a toothless crocodile. The pattern held with China. After imposing up to nearly 150% tariffs on Chinese goods on “Liberation Day,” Trump found that China was not, in fact, down. It struck back with export limits on rare earths. Trump was flummoxed.
As Anja Manuel, a former State Department official, told the Wall Street Journal, China “stood up to President Trump with the rare earths, and the U.S. backed down.” Trump quietly reversed several of the tariffs and then announced the result as a great “deal” after meeting with Xi.
Trump was more blase about threats from China than most members of the Republican and Democratic parties were. In 2024, large majorities of both parties voted for the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, a law that would require TikTok, a Chinese-owned company subject to state controls, to be sold. In his first term, Trump had labeled TikTok a grave national security threat, but when he returned to office in January 2025, he (illegally) suspended enforcement of the law. The legislators, and even the Supreme Court, thought the app was a propaganda arm of the PRC and had concerns about the data it was collecting from its tens of millions of American users. But Trump apparently did his usual analysis of all matters great and small: Is it good for me? After concluding that it was, since many Trump supporters got their news from TikTok, he declined to enforce the law and later arranged for TikTok to be sold to a consortium of Trump cronies.
Hot rhetoric notwithstanding, Trump has persistently retreated from substantive policies that would have signaled actual seriousness to China. Boasting of his “great relationship” with Xi, Trump froze a planned $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, signaled that he might lift sanctions on Chinese companies that bought Iranian oil and canceled defense talks with Taiwan. Though he didn’t do it to please the Chinese strongman, Trump surely made Xi smile when he withdrew several carrier groups from the South China Sea to redeploy to the Middle East after launching his war on Iran.
On top of this pattern of laxity, the Nvidia story represents a direct betrayal of U.S. national security — one so enormous that you have to reach for fiction for analogies. A president has a mental health meltdown? A Chinese mole makes it to the Oval Office? For two years now, the world has been transfixed by the potential threat of AI. It’s practically all we talk about. Everyone in the free world understands that in the race to dominate the industry, the U.S. and China are locked in competition. Perhaps the doomers are wrong to think the fate of humanity hangs in the balance, but at least we know that it’s kind of important that with a technology so powerful that it might upend everything, it’s better that the Chinese Communist Party not get ahead of us.
The advanced computer chips Nvidia manufactures are key to command and control, surveillance, the generation of deepfakes and much more. That’s the risk that permitting export of those chips poses for national security. What was Trump’s interest? Well, Nvidia powers the AI companies that are currently driving the stock market boom. Trump has personally invested between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock, and he doubtless appreciated Jensen Huang’s contribution of $25 million for the White House ballroom. So when Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent, the secretaries of state and the treasury, objected that Howard Lutnick, the secretary of commerce, is not enforcing export controls on Nvidia chips, it put Trump in a tough spot. On one hand, you have national security and the need to protect America from Chinese acquisition of the most sensitive technology in the world; on the other, you have Trump’s personal fortune possibly increasing through Nvidia’s success in selling to everyone, China included. It’s a tough choice, right?
Trump is worse than weak. He is, and has always been, for sale. We didn’t need the Nvidia scandal to prove this. If there is a conflict between Trump’s personal interest in vacuuming up cash and the national interest, his personal interest will prevail. Every single time.
This week’s summit provides yet another opportunity for Trump to hone his “great relationships” with the world’s worst dictators. It’s also an opportunity for the Democrats, who will soon gain the gavels in Congress, to reflect that they are the bulwark of national security now.
Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast. Her book, “Hard Right: The GOP’s Drift Toward Extremism,” is available now.

articles.title_orig: Scott Bessent Calls on Nvidia to Provide Answers on Chip Sales to China
articles.title_zh: Scott Bessent Calls on Nvidia to Provide Answers on Chip Sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a May 2026 ceremony in China. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.
Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.
Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.
Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."
For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.
What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

articles.title_orig: US intelligence says China accessed restricted American AI chips
articles.title_zh: US intelligence says China accessed restricted American AI chips
articles.content_orig:
Congressional watchdog leaders Randall Schriver and Mike Kuiken warn China could exploit American chips and AI to strengthen its military.
China's military could exploit advanced American technology, including through espionage and unauthorized access to artificial intelligence infrastructure, to develop weapons that could ultimately threaten U.S. forces, two congressional China watchdog leaders warned in an interview with Fox News Digital.
The officials raised concerns that Beijing is seeking to acquire sophisticated U.S. semiconductors and access powerful AI data centers, potentially strengthening its military capabilities without the knowledge or involvement of the American companies behind the technology.
Those concerns are underscored by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission's 2026 annual report , which says Beijing is seeking to circumvent American export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors for military modernization.
BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN
Racks of GPUs with a closed-loop liquid cooling system are seen inside an operational Microsoft data center in Indonesia on Feb. 4, 2026. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images)
Citing an April 2026 assessment by Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, the commission reported that China's People's Liberation Army was soliciting advanced Nvidia chips for AI-enabled military capabilities.
The report describes Beijing's push toward "intelligentized warfare," integrating AI into weapons systems, targeting, military command and logistics.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, warned that the threat extends beyond chip exports to access to computing infrastructure abroad. "Anytime the Chinese gain access to advanced chips, we are helping them," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
Commission Chairman Randall Schriver acknowledged the risk, pointing to permitted sales of dual-use technology, inadequate cybersecurity protections and American investments.
"I think we need sort of a comprehensive look at how the Americans are either wittingly or unwittingly contributing to Chinese military modernization," Schriver said.
Kuiken warned that Chinese AI developers or military institutions could also gain access to powerful data centers. "If we're doing it knowingly, we need to bring it to an end," he said.
TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed the Trump administration to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to China, making the company’s technology a focal point in the U.S.-China race for AI leadership. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The warnings come amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's relationship with China . Reuters reported Nov. 18, 2026, that Nvidia had stopped shipping licensed Hopper-generation AI data center chips to Chinese customers, according to interim CEO Colette Kress.
The findings also come amid a separate controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned in November following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , whom U.S. authorities have suspected of having intelligence ties to Beijing.
Jensen Huang has denied knowing about her alleged intelligence connections, while Beijing has rejected the espionage accusations. Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation. U.S. authorities have not conclusively established that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing, and Fox News Digital could not independently verify the allegations.
The commissioners also warned that China's advances extend beyond acquiring American hardware.
"Denial and deception is part of the CCP's standing doctrine, and that extends to the PLA, so I'm sure there are things we have yet to discover," Schriver said.
FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL
He pointed to China's growing use of AI-enabled military systems, including autonomous unmanned platforms.
Kuiken warned that Beijing is increasingly integrating advanced AI into existing military technology. "We are absolutely seeing the PLA take the technologies that they have on the shelf today and figuring out how they can deploy the most advanced artificial intelligence capabilities into that ecosystem so that they can gain advantage," he said.
Against those concerns, China's Foreign Ministry struck a more cooperative tone regarding AI security in a Nov. 19, 2026, statement following a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
China's first AI-powered soccer tournament (CCTV)
CHINA WATCHDOG WARNS TRUMP FACES ‘2-ON-1’ SHOWDOWN WITH XI, PUTIN AS TAIWAN RISKS MOUNT
"China and the United States should strengthen communication and coordination, prevent the security risks of AI, and ensure that AI is always under human control," the ministry said in its account of Xi's remarks.
The commission also identifies protecting American data as a leading national security priority, warning that AI could make it easier to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities and compromise sensitive information, amid a series of high-profile technology outages affecting major U.S. companies and government systems.
Asked about the recent disruptions involving the NSA, Apple and Chase Bank, Kuiken warned that increasingly sophisticated AI models are making it easier to identify cybersecurity weaknesses .
"These frontier models are incredibly good at cyber, which means they're good at coding and coding means it's very easy to find vulnerabilities in things," Kuiken told Fox News Digital. "You're basically seeing these leading organizations around the world do everything they can to lock down their organizations to make sure they're not vulnerable."
Kuiken emphasized that the commission's leading recommendation this year focuses on protecting American data, describing it as both a national security priority and an economic resource. "One, we want to protect it to keep ourselves secure and two, we wanna deploy it in the models that we have with the democratic world, controls to get economic benefit from it," he said.
The commissioners did not establish any connection between the recent technology outages and Chinese cyber operations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
An Amazon Web Services data center on Aug. 26, 2026, in Stone Ridge, Virginia. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended Beijing's technological development and criticized U.S. export restrictions. "China’s sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation," the spokesperson said. "China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues, opposes abuse of export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serve no one’s interests."
"China and the U.S. need to work together to deliver on the important common understandings between the two presidents and uphold the momentum of steady development of China-U.S. economic and trade ties," the spokesperson added.
The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.
Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict , global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump China Putin Jinping
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump China Putin Jinping
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.title_zh: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.content_orig:
EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey .
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”
after newsletter promotion
Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño , the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

articles.title_orig: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

articles.title_orig: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
articles.title_zh: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
articles.content_orig:
Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port early on Sunday morning
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Russian attack near Ukraine’s capital strikes apartment building, killing 3 and burying others
articles.title_zh: Russian attack near Ukraine’s capital strikes apartment building, killing 3 and burying others
articles.content_orig:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan ‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

articles.title_orig: F.A.A. Says All Delta Flights Through Atlanta Delayed as Automated System Falters
articles.title_zh: F.A.A. Says All Delta Flights Through Atlanta Delayed as Automated System Falters
articles.content_orig:
Delta Air Lines flights are facing delays nationwide after problems with systems that calculate takeoff weights and ensure safe aircraft settings, according to a Federal Aviation Administration advisory.
Video above: Could AI’s discovery of software flaws lead to more outages?
Delta teams are working to restore automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations, a company spokesperson told WSB-TV in a statement.
The company said it is using "manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed" while continuing to work on the automation issue.
"We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta told the outlet.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft is a critical part of the pre-departure preparations and ensures the fully loaded aircraft is not too heavy to fly, is loaded properly and the pilots have the right settings for a safe takeoff.
Major airlines use sophisticated computer programs at their headquarters to calculate these numbers.
The Delta slowdowns come at the outset of what is projected to be a busy holiday travel period. Over four million travelers are expected at Delta's largest hub in Atlanta, already the busiest airport in the world, between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1, according to a news release from the airport.
Many travelers have already experienced long lines and frustrating disruptions in recent weeks after all flights nationwide were grounded just over a week ago, sparking flight delays and cancellations for several days.
The FAA has said the outages that triggered the nationwide ground stop likely stemmed from an outdated copper wire at a remote location.
Sunday's Delta delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems, the FAA confirmed in a social media post .
"Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline's weight and balance system," the agency said, advising people to check with Delta for updates.
The ground delay affected Delta flights and was not airport-wide, a spokesperson for Hartsfield-Jackson told CNN in a statement. The airport said Delta is managing the issue.
CNN has reached out to Delta for more information.
Over 400 flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson were delayed Sunday afternoon, according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware, while slightly fewer inbound flights to the airport were also delayed. The data does not specify how many of these delays were Delta flights.
Atlanta resident Shane Rocha and her family were traveling through Hartsfield-Jackson this morning to visit family, Rocha told CNN affiliate WANF. Rocha said she had flown earlier this week without any issues and was hoping that today's travel would be equally smooth.
"Luckily we're only 19 minutes delayed, knock on wood," she said. "Hopefully it stays that low."
Although the specifics surrounding the Delta issue remain unclear, United Airlines experienced an issue with its weight and balance computer system in 2025 that triggered more than 1,000 delays and dozens of cancellations, the airport said at the time.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey — International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions .
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.
The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits .
A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: How Kim Jong Un Gets Away With Building Nukes and Ghosting Trump
articles.title_zh: How Kim Jong Un Gets Away With Building Nukes and Ghosting Trump
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has attempted to re-establish dialogue and even arrange a summit with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jong-Un since his re-election to office.
Last year, Trump attempted to reach his North Korean through established communications channels between Washington and Pyongyang, but nobody on the North Korean end of the line responded. The president subsequently wrote a letter that was delivered to a North Korean UN diplomat. The letter was returned unopened.
Finally, Trump tried to set up a meeting with the North Korean dictator during his recent visit to Asia , where he held a landmark high-profile summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin . The hermetic Asian state reportedly set terms for the potential meeting that the White House could not accept.
The various instances of Washington reaching out to Pyongyang were revealed by the Wall Street Journal on Saturday. The Journal also reported that Kim is now pushing the U.S. to recognize North Korea as a legitimate nuclear power.
During Trump's first term in office, the president met Kim three times, in Singapore, Vietnam and the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) respectively. During the final meeting, Trump even briefly stepped onto North Korean soil.
The first meeting between the two in Singapore in June 2018 marked the first time a sitting U.S. president had met a North Korean leader, and was hailed as a diplomatic moment of paramount importance.
Despite the three meetings, no new deal on North Korean denuclearization, which was seen as Washington's ultimate objective, was reached.
Nevertheless, tensions between the two traditional adversaries did temporarily cool, but soon ratcheted up again after negotiations failed in 2019 and North Korea began conducting full-range ICBM test launches after a several-year moratorium and joint U.S.-South Korean military drills, which had been paused, also restarted.
Far from denuclearizing, North Korea's nuclear stockpile has grown significantly since Trump and Kim last met. Estimates suggest that, at the time of the two leaders' meeting in the Korean DMZ, North Korea possessed 20-30 nuclear warheads , a figure that has increased to about 60 at the time of writing.
U.S. intelligence also concluded in 2025 that "Kim has no intention of negotiating away his strategic weapons programs."
Accepting this fact, according to Kim, is the key to securing lasting peace between the U.S. and North Korea.
"If the U.S. respects the present position of our state specified in the Constitution of the DPRK and withdraws its hostile policy toward the DPRK, there is no reason why we cannot get on well with the U.S.," the North Korean strongman said in February. North Korea's status as a nuclear power was enshrined in a constitutional amendment enacted in 2023.

articles.title_orig: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.title_zh: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.content_orig:
Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument
The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.
The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.
Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.
“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.
As artificial intelligence has grown exponentially in recent years, militaries and manufacturers have created increasingly advanced weapons systems for both offensive and defensive purposes.
These systems include the use of AI in generating target banks , as was done by the Israeli military in Gaza, as well as semi-autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war, which have “last-mile capability”, where AI takes over in the drone’s final approach to its target.
The president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres, have called for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on use of weapons. In particular, the ICRC has called for a ban on the use of autonomous weapons against personnel, as well as ensuring that weapons systems behave predictably and placing limits on weapons including restricting their use to military objectives.
Experts have said that given the rapid development of autonomous weapons and AI, the failure to create adequate regulations could have dangerous repercussions.
“It’s not about banning all autonomous weapon systems, but to set limits in an international treaty of red lines that should never be crossed,” said Droege. “We’re very close to crossing those red lines, particularly targeting human beings through machines should be a moral red line.”
Other rights groups warned that any delay towards regulation of these weapons risked allowing private industry and militaries to set the norms of how autonomous weapons are used.
Already, autonomous weapons have led to civilian harm. Three civilians were killed by a Russian drone guided by an AI system in July in Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine. The drone tried to hit a petrol station, probably its intended target, but instead crashed into a wall, killing three people in a fountain of shrapnel.
In Gaza, Israel has used AI-assisted targeting methods to fill its target banks much faster than humanly possible since the start of the war. As a result, rights groups have said that civilians and people with tenuous links to militant groups were erroneously killed.
In Iran, a US strike that hit an elementary school, killing 156 civilians including 120 schoolchildren, reportedly was a result of faulty intelligence gathered by AI systems.
Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said further delay to a strong treaty could see “more cases of mass civilian harm that we’ve seen over the past 18 months to two years”, warning that some of these mass casualty events could dwarf what has already occurred. She said manufacturers and militaries were trying to develop “swarm” capabilities, where hundreds or thousands of autonomous drones act at the same time.
“This has the potential for high damage, just because of the sheer mass of systems that would be autonomous. All it takes is for one of them to face algorithmic error and then the entire swarm is utilised and led down a path based on that error … particularly if they’re programmed to target humans.”
There is also a risk of proliferation, as non-state groups increasingly use AI to program their weapons systems, as was the case when the Houthi movement in Yemen used Claude to “vibe code” ballistic missiles.
Armed Islamist groups in Africa’s Sahel region have reportedly used AI tools to improve drone ballistics and for operational planning.
“This is the only thing that is important this week. It’s not really the substance of laws. What’s on the agenda here, after 13 years, is the political will finally present to start to get serious about regulation of autonomous weapons systems,” said a senior diplomat with knowledge of the UN discussions.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Is Racing to Keep Its Booming Defense Industry From Stalling
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Is Racing to Keep Its Booming Defense Industry From Stalling
articles.content_orig:
“If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately,” says Igor Nakonechnyi. The CEO of Project Foundation, a Ukrainian bid to build chip capacity in Europe, tells EU Perspectives why the drone industry depends on China and what Europe can learn from Ukraine’s frontline.
The war in Ukraine has exposed how heavily the world’s drone industry relies on China for critical components . The Fourth Law is a Ukrainian defence technology company that develops autonomous drones for use on the battlefield.
Together with its sister company Odd Systems, which supplies drone cameras, it is working to establish semiconductor manufacturing capacity in Europe through an initiative called Project Foundation. The two firms want to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers and address a vulnerability that affects Ukraine’s drone industry and Europe’s wider security.
In the interview, Igor Nakonechnyi describes the daily struggle to source components amid sudden shortages and price hikes. He also explains why the company is opening an R&D hub in Eindhoven, why many EU funding programmes take too long to pay out, and why the Chips Act should cover dual-use technologies.
Our company was created in response to Russian aggression. Our team already had quite some experience in entrepreneurship and consumer electronics, so they were looking at how they could best use their skills in the face of the aggression.
Drones are a defining feature of modern warfare. One of the key components of a drone is a camera. Basically, they are the eyes of the drone.
The real bottleneck here is the thermal sensor — a semiconductor chip that allows a camera to detect heat. China can make around 20 million of those a year. Every thermal drone needs a sensor, so whoever controls sensors controls how many thermal drones can be built.
Outside China, it is pretty much only North America and France that have some manufacturing capacity, which is maybe a couple of million in total. That’s a huge discrepancy, and we see it as a huge vulnerability.
Indeed. If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately.
Even if we haven’t yet seen a full restriction, there’s already always a shortage of specific things, or the price suddenly goes up. — Igor Nakonechnyi, CEO of Project Foundation
Even if we haven’t yet seen a full restriction, there’s already always a shortage of specific things, or the price suddenly goes up. It’s a constant challenge that our procurement team deals with on a daily basis.
That’s a critical vulnerability that we want to solve not only for Ukraine, but also for Europe and the rest of the world. That’s exactly why we launched Project Foundation, to build thermal-sensor fabs in Europe and the US, so the West no longer depends on China for the eyes of its drones.
We are currently setting up a subsidiary in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, where Project Foundation is headquartered and will serve as one of our main R&D hubs.
We see ourselves as part of Europe. And we see a lot of opportunities and talent in Europe to build this with.
I see that a lot of relevant stakeholders already understand this, and more and more are becoming aware. In the US, even more so: more money is being invested in sovereign production, specifically of military equipment. This has always been the case, but investment is growing even more now. In Europe, it’s gradually getting better.
To be clear: my company does not receive any EU funding at the moment. But we are looking at a few funding calls.
However, we see that many funding programmes have timelines that are simply too slow for us. If you want to apply for funding, it can easily take a year before you actually get it. So you need to write a project, wait almost a year until you get the money, and then you have two or three years to build a prototype.
Even within a year, warfare in Ukraine will have changed completely, and the concept you requested funding for might no longer be relevant. — Igor Nakonechnyi
That timeframe doesn’t match modern warfare. Even within a year, warfare in Ukraine will have changed completely, and the concept you requested funding for might no longer be relevant.
There are more agile programmes coming, but we need more of them. We really need more speed.
Yes, that’s a very good initiative, but a big problem for us is that it’s primarily for civil use and not dual use. For example, what we are working towards—thermal-camera sensors or image sensors—is not really part of the Chips Act, whereas we believe it is an important topic.
We are talking about semiconductor manufacturing here, so it makes sense from that perspective. We do already see dual use in, for example, the Industrial Accelerator Act [a proposed EU law aimed at boosting manufacturing and demand for European-made and low-carbon products].
The reality of today’s world is that many different things are interlinked. Embracing dual use in, for example, the Chips Act would reflect that reality.
Our company is originally driven by demand in Ukraine, but we of course want a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. And that peace only lasts when there’s a strong, independent defence industry behind it to deter another war. We hope to continue contributing to that; not only for Ukraine but for the wider Western world.
We see ourselves as a global company, and also hope to use our products in civilian applications in the future, such as consumer robotics and cars. We don’t want this to end up only in the hands of China.

articles.title_orig: Yardeni Cuts S&P 500 Target Again, Says Bear Market Is Unlikely
articles.title_zh: Yardeni Cuts S&P 500 Target Again, Says Bear Market Is Unlikely
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 entered correction territory after U.S. stocks fell 3.7% Friday, leaving the index more than 10% below its recent peak after it broke its 200-day moving average. Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research and one of Wall Street’s biggest bulls, said the selloff has gone too far and is a correction rather than a bear market, according to BeInCrypto.
Yardeni cited healthy corporate earnings and cheaper valuations, and still expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,500–9,000 by the end of 2027, though he sees no immediate trigger for a sharp recovery. Last year’s Liberation Day crash reversed after Trump changed course on tariffs, but investors may have to wait longer for a rebound this time. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said inflation remains a serious concern and raised the possibility of a half-point rate hike in December; markets expect further hikes in December and January. UBS strategist David Lefkowitz also expects slower growth and weaker AI spending. U.S. consumer sentiment rose roughly 7% in November to its highest level since August. Upcoming inflation data and December’s Fed decision will test whether rate hikes push the economy toward recession and undermine Yardeni’s recovery outlook.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.content_orig:
Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices.
In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the US-Iran war began in late February.
As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data. The reporting area covers the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
Before October, the number of reported attacks in the region averaged around 10 per month. Numbers vary, but data from the International Maritime Organization also points to October as having the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year.
Since the conflict began, the strait has become a heavily contested frontier , with attacks there disrupting oil and gas shipping and sparking global economic fallout.
Iran began trying to halt traffic in the wake of the US-Israeli attacks that launched the war. In response, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and as CNN previously reported , Gulf producers have found ways of getting ships through the strait.
Commercial traffic through the channel – through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war – remains at a reduced level when compared to the 2025 baseline.
As global oil prices fall and the Iran’s domestic crude revenues come under increasing strain, Tehran has been stepping up attacks, with experts saying the country is losing its leverage over the waterway and could escalate attacks further in an attempt to force concessions from Washington.
The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports. Prices also fell after the US midterm results as concerns over fresh US military action in the Middle East subsided.
“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN . “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s domestic oil revenues are falling sharply as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to stifle the country’s supply of oil to global markets, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler.
“Iranian oil on water outside the (US) blockade zone has hit zero as the last cargoes discharged in China earlier this month. Consequently, Iran’s oil revenues could drop to zero by mid-December,” Kpler reported in late October.
US President Donald Trump said this month the US doesn’t “need a deal” with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere .
“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
He later indicated he wouldn’t hesitate to resume military strikes in Iran if necessary.
During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to Marisks, a maritime risk management company.
Marisks did not confirm who was behind the attacks, though it said Iranian involvement was “assessed as likely.”
Trump says Iran is ‘bullsh*tting’ on effort to end war
Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow at 3 p.m. UTC (10 a.m. ET) on Friday. All crew were reported safe, Marisks said.
The Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged crude oil tanker, caught fire after being hit in the stern at 5 a.m. UTC on Saturday (midnight ET on Saturday). Less than an hour later, the Arina, also Hong Kong-flagged, was struck in the engine room by a missile.
The attacks demonstrate the “continued critical threat” to commercial shipping in the region, Marisks said, particularly through the “southern corridor” near Oman’s coastline which Iran vehemently opposes.
CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Laura Sharman, Nadeen Ebrahim and Alayna Treene contributed reporting.
